title: Aggressive Italian Game
description: A powerful opening repertoire in 1.e4 e5, based on many central gambits such as the Max Lange, Deutz, and Double Knight. Better for intermediate and advanced players as there is more memorization, but available to all levels.

2kr2r1/p1p1qpPp/2p1b3/8/2p5/5Q2/PPP2PPP/.text:
We are moving away from the attack and are attacking the c6 pawn. 

We want to continue by finishing our development.

If you are able to evaluate the position, you'll notice White is better because of king safety, piece activity and structure!

2kr2r1/p1p1qpPp/2p1b3/8/2p5/8/PPP2PPP/RN.text: Black can't take our queen, because we would have the intermezzo of Nxe7+ prior to capturing their rook. Thus Black has to capture and accept a completely demolished queen-side pawn structure.

2kr2r1/ppp1qpPp/2n1b3/8/2pN4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black thinks they can castle and pin our knight. 

Is this so? Pause the study and try to find the winning move!

3rk1r1/ppp1qpPp/2n1b3/8/2pN4/2P5/PP3PPP/.text:
A simple yet effective way to defend our knight. 

In the next few moves we will develop our queen and remaining knight, and if Black takes on d4, we'll recapture with the c3-pawn.

3rk1r1/ppp1qpPp/2n1b3/8/2pN4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
This is the best response for Black.

Black attacks and pins our d4-knight but does not allow tricky jumps.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text:
Besides 3...Nf6, the main way to continue. Black wants to maintain control over the d4 square.

We want to castle as soon as possible! 

Firstly, we want to bring our king into safety and then play aggressively.

r1bqk1r1/ppp1bpPp/2n5/8/2pp4/5N2/PPP2PPP.text: 9...Be7 will transpose to the main line with 9...Be6 after our reply of Bg5.

r1bqk1r1/ppp2pPp/2n5/2b5/2pp4/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
The only available square for Black's rook is g8.

Let's give check! We activate our pieces!

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n2P2/2b5/2pp4/5N2/PPP2P.text:
A forced move, however, lots of lower-rated players will be uneasy with us taking the g7 pawn.

We'll grab it and hit the rook!

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/2bpP3/2Bp4/5N2/PPP.text:
6...d5 is Black's best attempt to fight off our attack. 

However, d5 is not the easiest move to find and leads to complicated positions.

We are now reaching forcing variations  with multiple captures, the first of which is on f6. We take the knight.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/P.text:
Again, the most popular continuation. Black attacks the e4-pawn and prepares to castle short.

We'll play the striking move d4! 
We are using the fact that we have an extra starting move, and our king has already castled. 

Black has to "waste" a move to capture the d4-pawn. For the price of the d-pawn, we will get more space in the center and will be able to develop faster.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2BpP3/5N2/PPP.text:
After 5...exd4, we have officially entered Max Lange Attack territory.

With e5, we strike in the center right away! 

Black already has a big problem on their hands. Finding the right move isn't easy. On the other hand, our position is easy to navigate.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
By far the most common reply for Black. Black is defending the attacked e5-pawn and developing the knight at the same time.

With Bc4, we reach one of the most famous openings in chess - the Italian Game. From beginners to the World Champion, everyone plays it. 

The bishop targets the f7-pawn and controls d5, rarely allowing Black counterplay in the center.

r2q2r1/ppp1k1Pp/2n1b3/5p2/2pp3R/5N2/PPP2.text:
But we can put the rook to h4! Now, instead of having one threat, now we have two! We are threatening both the h7 and the d4 pawn. Black is not able to defend both. 

After we capture a pawn, we want to continue by developing our queenside.

r2q2r1/ppp1k1Pp/2n1b3/5p2/2ppR3/5N2/PPP2.text: Black is simply trying to distract our rook.

r2q2r1/ppp1kpPp/2n1b3/8/2p1R3/3p1N2/PPP2.text:
This pawn advance is another way for Black to defend the d-pawn.

By playing d3, Black weakened the c4-pawn. We are threatening to capture it after we play Nd2.

r2q2r1/ppp1kpPp/2n1b3/8/2p1R3/5N2/PPQN1P.text:
A position one can truly dream of. 

The c4 pawn is about to fall, and we are only one move away from our last piece entering the game. 

Black's king will be stuck in the center for a long time. Our chances are great in this position!

r2q2r1/ppp1kpPp/2n1b3/8/2p1R3/5N2/PPpN1P.text: This move doesn't really help Black much.

r2q2r1/ppp1kpPp/2n1b3/8/2pp4/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
Black wants to retain the defense of the d4-pawn.

We'll play very dynamically. 

Instead of developing the remaining pieces, we lift our Rook and threaten to capture the d4-pawn.

r2qk1r1/ppp1BpPp/2n1b3/8/2pp4/5N2/PPP2PP.text: We have transposed to the 9...Be6 line.

r2qk1r1/ppp1bpPp/2n1b3/6B1/2pp4/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black protects their queen from attack and tries to remain solid.

We'll exchange bishops. Now it will be challenging for Black to defend the dark squares.

r2qk1r1/ppp2pPp/2n1b3/2b5/2pp4/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Black blocks the e-file with the light-squared bishop. 

Black dreams about having time to develop their queen and castle long.

With Bg5, we continue to pose problems. Sometimes our idea can be to put the g5-bishop on f6, reinforcing the g7-pawn and paralyzing the g8-rook.

r3k1r1/ppp1bpPp/2n1b3/5qB1/2ppN3/5N2/PPP.text:
The only way to stop Nf6+.

But after the dark-squared bishops are exchanged, it will be much harder for Black to control the dark squares.

Also, there is no way for Black to defend the d4-pawn.

r3k1r1/ppp1qpPp/2n1b3/8/2pp4/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
With 11...Qe7, Black gives the d4-pawn but prepares to take control over the d-file. 

We'll take on d4 with our knight.

r3k1r1/ppp2pPp/2n1b3/2b2qB1/2pp4/2N2N2/P.text:
Black is not happy to move the queen again, but there is no other option.

The f5 square is the only sensible square.

We'll play Ne4, threatening a lethal fork on f6.

r3k1r1/ppp2pPp/2n1b3/2bq2B1/2pp4/5N2/PPP.text:
Simply put, this is a blunder.

Black did not want to retreat the c5-bishop, but their queen is now a target.

Let's attack it with Nc3! Black cannot take the c3-knight as the queen is unprotected because of the pinned e6-bishop.

r3k3/ppp2prp/2n1b3/2b2qB1/2ppN2N/8/PPP2P.text:
That's all she wrote! 

Black loses the queen after Nf6+ on the next move.

r3k3/ppp2prp/2n1b3/2b2qB1/2ppN3/5N2/PPP2.text: If the rook takes the pawn...

r5r1/ppp1kpPp/2n1b3/5q2/2pNN3/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
We are capturing the d4-pawn and attacking the queen on f5. 

Our position is much easier to play as we have a safer king. 

In the next few moves, we will want to develop our queen and the a1-rook.

r5r1/ppp1kpPp/2n1b3/5q2/2ppN3/5N2/PPP2PP.text: Taking with the knight would leave the d4 square completely undefended.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
The most popular reply for Black.

With our response of Nf3, we are developing a piece, controlling the center, attacking the e5-pawn and are one move closer to castling.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the Max Lange Attack! 

Consider this chapter an introduction to the ideas of the Max Lange Attack: swift development with Nf3/Bc4 and a pawn push: d4!

Let's get the chapter under way with our opening move, 1.e4. "Best by test" - Bobby Fischer.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1P3/2Bp4/5N2/PPP.text:
Black decides it is best to put their knight back in the stable. 

Unfortunately for Black, that's rarely a good way to continue. Falling behind on piece development usually leads to easy wins.

We'll keep up the pressure and attack f7 by playing Ng5.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text:
Besides 3...Nf6, the main way to continue. Black wants to maintain control over the d4 square.

We want to castle as soon as possible! 

Firstly, we want to bring our king into safety and then play aggressively.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n5/2bpP3/2Bpn3/5N2/PPP1.text: A last attempt to save the e4-knight.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2nP4/2b5/2Bpn3/5N2/PPP1Q.text:
But we can take en passant and the knight is still hanging.

We will continue with Bg5 and Nbd2, putting maximum pressure on Black's position.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/P.text:
Again, the most popular continuation. Black attacks the e4-pawn and prepares to castle short.

We'll play the striking move d4! 
We are using the fact that we have an extra starting move, and our king has already castled. 

Black has to "waste" a move to capture the d4-pawn. For the price of the d-pawn, we will get more space in the center and will be able to develop faster.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2BpP3/5N2/PPP.text:
After 5...exd4, we have officially entered Max Lange Attack territory.

With e5, we strike in the center right away! 

Black already has a big problem on their hands. Finding the right move isn't easy. On the other hand, our position is easy to navigate.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n4n/2b1P1N1/2Bp4/8/PPP.text: The only sensible way to defend the f7-pawn.

A simple yet deadly move. 

We are not allowing Black to move the d-pawn because their king is stuck on the e-file, and we would just take the pawn, with a discovered check from the rook. 

On the other hand, if Black decides to castle, Black will be met by a deadly Qd3 surprise.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1P3/2Bp1Bn1/5N2/P.text: We are protecting the e5-pawn and are getting ready to bring more pieces into the game. Some of our next moves can be Re1, Nd2, and h3.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1P3/2Bp2n1/5N2/PP.text: Black's attacking the e5-pawn, but the g4-knight is a little misplaced.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1P3/2Bpn3/5N2/PPP.text:
A game-losing blunder. 

We simply play Qe2, and Black will not be able to defend the e4-knight. Often you will see this mistake. Moves similar to this one are often the main continuation, followed by reinforcement from pawns.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
By far the most common reply for Black. Black is defending the attacked e5 pawn and developing the knight at the same time.

With Bc4, we reach one of the most famous openings in chess - the Italian Game. From beginners to the World Champion, everyone plays it. 

The bishop targets the f7-pawn and controls d5, rarely allowing Black counterplay in the center.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
The most popular reply for Black.

With our response of Nf3, we are developing a piece, controlling the center, attacking the e5 pawn and are one move closer to castling.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this chapter of the Max Lange Attack we'll analyze other moves after Black takes the pawn on d4. 

What if we play e5, and Black moves their knight to some other square? 

In this study, we'll answer that question! Let's begin with our opening move, 1.e4. "Best by test" - Bobby Fischer.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text:
Besides 3...Nf6, the main way to continue. Black wants to maintain the control over the d4 square.

We want to castle as soon as possible! 

Firstly, we want to bring our king to safety and then play aggressively.

r1bqk1r1/ppp2pPp/2n5/8/2pp4/8/PPP2PPP/RN.text:
The only available square for Black's rook is g8.

We'll play Re1+, and we can clearly see why this line is so bad for Black. Without the dark-squared bishop, Black does not have the option of retreating it to e7.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n2P2/8/2pp4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
The only move.

We'll grab the g7-pawn with an attack on the h8-rook. Black has to react, giving us time to continue energetically.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3pP3/2Bp4/8/PPP2PP.text:
As we have seen in previous chapters, d5 is Black's best try in this type of position. After this move, we enter a forced sequence.

We will capture on g7 and bring our pieces into the game.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/P.text:
Again, the most popular continuation.

Black's attacking the e4-pawn and getting ready to castle short.

And just like the previous chapter, we strike in the center with many of the same ideas!

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2BbP3/5N2/PPP.text:
5... Bxd4 is the most solid way to continue for Black. Also, it has been played in the majority of master games. Black's idea is to keep the center structure intact.
 
But taking with the bishop on d4 also has its downsides. We can capture it immediately and seize the bishop pair.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/2BpP3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
Taking on d4 with the pawn is a big mistake. Black has transposed to a worse version of the Max Lange Gambit. Also, in a way, it defeats the purpose of Black's last move. The whole idea of giving the bishop pair was to maintain the structure.

We'll play energetically, and push forward with e5.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
By far the most common reply for Black. Black is defending the attacked e5 pawn and developing the knight at the same time.

With Bc4, we reach one of the most famous openings in chess - the Italian Game.

r2qk1r1/ppp2pPp/2n1b3/8/2pp4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black blocks the e-file with the light-squared bishop. Black dreams of having time to develop the queen and castle long.

Now 11. Qh5 is the crucial move that secures our advantage. We threaten to take on e6 because the f7-pawn is pinned. Also, we have a very strong threat of Bg5 attacking the queen and cutting the black king off from the queenside.

r3k1r1/ppp2pP1/2n1bBp1/8/2pp4/8/PPP2PPP/.text: Our bishop is protecting the g7-pawn and still cuts the black king off from castling queen side. In the next few moves, we will develop the rest of our queen side pieces. We claim that Black's c4- and d4- pawns are weaknesses rather than strengths.

r3k1r1/ppp2pPp/2n1b1q1/6BQ/2pp4/8/PPP2PP.text:
The only sensible move for Black. A similar position could occur if instead of 12...Qg6, Black played 12...Qf5 13.g4 Qg6.

The best way for us to continue is to enter an endgame. We have a strong, passed g7-pawn and well-positioned pieces.

r3k1r1/ppp2pPp/2n1bq2/7Q/2pp4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
With Qf6, Black protects the e6-bishop but also has an idea to take on g7 and threaten checkmate, or to play Qg6 to try and exchange queens.

We'll play Bg5, a developing move that makes sure we are on top. Black's dreams of castling long are only that - dreams. Black must handle problems on the kingside.

r3k1r1/ppp2pqp/2n1b3/6BQ/2pp4/8/PPP2PPP/.text: Eliminating the pawn, but forgetting that the queen was needed to protect the e6-bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
The most popular reply for Black.

With our response of Nf3, we are developing a piece, controlling the center, attacking the e5 pawn and are one move closer to castling.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the Deutz Gambit chapter! 

This is a very tricky line that will most often arise from the Giuoco Piano. With the rise of neural network engines Stockfish and Leela, the Deutz Gambit underwent a revival. 

From being rarely seen on the top level, now every top GM has to be ready for it.

Let's begin with our opening move, 1.e4. "Best by test" - Bobby Fischer.

r1b1k2r/ppp2p2/4P2p/3P2q1/2BQ2np/8/PPP3P.text: But with e6, we threaten both the h8-rook and a capture on f7. We stand very well, with a huge attack on the black king.

r1b1k2r/ppp2p2/7p/3PP1q1/2BQ2np/8/PPP3PP.text:
The queen protects the g4-knight. 

Also, Black would like to play Rg8 and try to arrange checkmate on g2.

r1b1k2r/ppp2p2/8/3qp1B1/3n4/8/PPP3PP/RN1.text:
We want to continue here by developing the knight. 

Our goal should be to get the knight to f6. Also, we want to develop our queen to d2 and bring the a1-rook into the game.

r1bk3r/ppp2p2/5P1p/8/2p1P2p/8/PPP3PP/RN3.text:
After all is said and done, we have an endgame where White is clearly better. 

While the material is balanced, Black's pawn structure is left in ruins. With doubled c- and h-pawns there isn't much hope. 

Our plan in this position is to develop the knight and attack the weak pawns with our rooks.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text:
Besides 3...Nf6, the main way to continue. Black wants to maintain the control over the d4 square.

We want to castle as soon as possible! 

Firstly, we want to bring our king to safety and then play aggressively.

r1bqk2r/ppp2p2/5n1p/3Pp3/2Bn1P1p/8/PPP3P.text:
Black takes our bishop.

We'll take on e5, after which both black knights are en prise.

r1bqk2r/ppp2p2/5n1p/3pP3/2BnP2p/8/PPP3PP.text:
Black's last chance to stay in the game is to go for a counterattack.

There are a few good options for us in this position, but Qxd4 is the simplest. 

We enter an endgame where we will have a clear advantage.

r1bqk2r/ppp2p2/5n1p/3pp1p1/2BnPP1B/8/PPP.text:
d5 is the best and the most energetic response for Black. 

However, this move is very sharp and not easy to find in a real game. 

Black's idea is to open up the c8-h3 diagonal. Besides that, Black gains an extra move to handle the position.

We'll take the d-pawn.

r1bqk2r/ppp2p2/5n1p/4P3/2pQP2p/8/PPP3PP/.text:
Black has to capture our bishop. Otherwise, we would capture on d5 with the e-pawn.

We'll exchange queens.

r1bqk2r/ppp2p2/7p/3PP3/2Bn2np/8/PPP3PP/R.text: Black can try to create a counterattack, but we'll capture on d4 and prevent the threat of Ne3.

r1bqk2r/ppp2p2/7p/3nP3/2Bn3p/8/PPP3PP/RN.text:
Besides playing Ng4, this is the only other move that makes sense. 

In fact, this is the better move because it also captures the d-pawn and centralizes the knight.

We'll capture on d4.

r1bqk2r/ppp2p2/7p/3np1p1/2Bn1P1B/8/PPP3P.text:
Nxd5 is the simplest way to continue.

At the same time, it is very decent considering Black's position. 

Black's f6-knight is no longer a target and the g5-pawn is now protected by the queen.

We'll take on g5, opening the f-file.

r1bqk2r/ppp2p2/8/3np1p1/2Bn3B/8/PPP3PP/R.text:
Black has to recapture.

Now, by exchanging on d5, we force Black's queen to move away from the defense of the g5-pawn.

r1bqk2r/pppp1p2/5n1p/4P3/2B2p1B/8/PPP1Q1.text:
Once again, e5 is the final blow! 

Black cannot defend the f6 Knight. After the next move, we will have two pieces for a rook. Our bishops are very active, and the game will not last long.

r1bqk2r/pppp1p2/5n1p/4p1p1/2BnP2B/8/PPP2.text:
g5 is the critical move in the position.

Black wants to push our bishop back to g3, and after d6 claim our bishop is semi-useless because it is hitting a pawn chain. 

Also, Black has a clamp over the f4 square, stopping our main idea.

But we'll play f4 anyway! It will come as a shock because the f4 square is covered twice.

r1bqk2r/pppp1p2/5n1p/4p3/2B1PR1B/8/PPP1n.text: Since Black will lose the knight anyway, Black argues that our queen is worse on e2 than it would be on d4.

r1bqk2r/pppp1p2/5n1p/4p3/2BnPP1p/8/PPP3P.text:
Most often, we will see this move played by a lower-rated player. 

Yes, Black did capture our bishop, but it is likely that our opponent did not calculate the line very well.

We'll take on e5. Both knights are now en prise, and f7 is under huge pressure.

r1bqk2r/pppp1p2/5n1p/4p3/2BnPp1B/8/PPP3P.text:
...gxf4 is the second most popular move at lower levels. 

Most often, players who have played this move feared falling into a trap after taking the h4-bishop. 

With this move, Black hopes to keep the position solid.

We'll play the stunning Rxf4, sacrificing our rook to blow the position open!

r1bqk2r/pppp1p2/5n1p/8/2BQPp1B/8/PPP3PP/.text: Black can not defend the f6-knight. Black's position is simply lost.

r1bqk2r/pppp1pp1/5n1p/4p1B1/2BnP3/8/PPP2.text:
Black is forcing us to declare on which diagonal we will keep our bishop.

There is also an idea to follow up ...h6 with ...g5 which has recently been very popular in all kinds of 1. e4 e5 positions.

We'll drop back to h4. Our idea is still the same: to keep the pressure on the f6-knight and push through with f4.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/P.text:
Again, the most popular continuation.

Black's attacking the e4-pawn and getting ready to castle short.

And just like in the previous chapter, we strike in the center with many of the same ideas!

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2BbP3/5N2/PPP.text:
5... Bxd4 is the most solid way to continue for Black. Also, it has been played in majority of master games. Black's idea is to keep the center structure intact.
 
But taking with the bishop on d4 also has its downsides. We can capture it immediately and seize the bishop pair.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/2BnP3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
Nxd4 is Black's best continuation. 

Black's structure remains solid. All in all, Black forces us to show why we have sacrificed the d-pawn.

By sacrificing the d-pawn, we are able to develop our bishop immediately.

Our idea is to put pressure on the f6-knight. In most lines, we will follow up by playing f4 and opening up the f-file.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
By far the most common reply for Black. Black is defending the attacked e5-pawn and developing the knight at the same time.

With Bc4, we reach one of the most famous openings in chess - the Italian Game.

r2qk2r/ppp2p2/4b2p/3nP3/2B4p/8/PPP2QPP/R.text:
We'll play Qf2, putting pressure on f7.

In this position, we should continue by exchanging our bishop for the knight, then playing Nc3 and Rad1.

Strategically, we would like to enter an endgame because Black has a lot of weak pawns.

It is easy to imagine that if there were no pieces on the board, our king could simply capture the h4 and h6 pawns.

r2qk2r/ppp2p2/4b2p/3nP3/2BQ3p/8/PPP3PP/R.text: Black protects the d5-knight and prepares to castle long.

r2qk2r/ppp2p2/5n1p/3Pp1p1/2B2PbB/8/PPn3P.text:
The most critical line.

Black forces us to show why we are giving up the a1-rook.

We'll take on e5 with check.

r2qk2r/ppp2p2/5n1p/3Pp1p1/2Bn1PbB/8/PPP3.text:
Bg4 is the most commonly played move in master games. 

Black wants to develop the bishop and gain a tempo on our queen.

We'll play Qe1, threatening to take the e5-pawn.

r3k2r/ppp1qp2/5n1p/3PQ1p1/2B2PbB/8/PPn3P.text:
Since the black king is in trouble, it makes sense for Black to offer the trade of queens.

But we can safely exchange, because the knight on f6 is going to turn out to be unfortunately placed.

r6r/ppp1kp2/5n1p/3P2P1/2B3bB/8/PPn3PP/RN.text:
This move solves all of our problems and shows we are better in this position. 

If Black continued by taking the a1-rook, we would be able to capture the f6-knight with a check and play our knight to a3. 

Black's a1-knight is trapped and we will pick it up on the next move.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
The most popular reply for Black.

With our response of Nf3, we are developing a piece, controlling the center, attacking the e5-pawn and are one move closer to castling.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the second study of the Deutz Gambit. 

We'll see what to do if Black captures on d4 with the knight after we trade on d4. 

Even some masters have been known to go for this variation, so pay close attention! 

Let's begin with our opening move, 1.e4. "Best by test" - Bobby Fischer.

r1bk1b1r/p1p2ppp/2p5/2n1P1B1/8/5N2/PPP2P.text: We develop the bishop with check - if Black blocks it with Be7, we'll trade and continue by developing our knight and castling queenside in order to connect the rooks and capitalize on our better pawn structure.

r1bq1b1r/ppp2kpp/2np4/4P3/4n3/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
Black has no better option than to go along with our plan.

We'll fork the king and knight with Qd5+.

r1bq1b1r/pppp1kpp/5n2/4p3/3nP3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Black has no better option than to go along with White's temporary bishop sacrifice.

We'll take on e5 with check, eliminating the defender of the d4-knight.

r1bq1bkr/pppp2pp/5n2/4N3/3QP3/8/PPP2PPP/.text: White regains the piece with interest. In the future, White will castle, finish their queenside development and then start harassing the weak black king.

r1bq1bkr/pppp2pp/5n2/4N3/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP/.text: Black runs back behind their pawns, where the king should be safe.

r1bq1rk1/ppppbppp/2n5/2n1P3/2B5/2N2N2/PP.text: Black brings their king into safety.

r1bq1rk1/ppppbppp/2n5/2nNP3/2B5/5N2/PPP2.text:
We centralize our knight, eyeing c7, which is only protected by the queen.

White should focus on finishing their development and then trying to attack the barely protected black king.

r1bqk2r/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/8/2BNP3/8/PPP2PP.text:
Black blocks the e-file and prepares to castle. 

The e4-pawn is now threatened, since Black can easily escape White's threats along the e-file.

White brings the rook out and protects the pawn on e4. 

In the next few moves, White will finish developing their queenside and connect the rooks.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1P3/2B1n3/5N2/PPP.text:
Black develops the bishop and attacks f2, hoping to gain some time to castle.

But we'll ignore the threat on f2 and threatens something even bigger - a checkmate on f7. 

Also, the knight on e4 is now hanging.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/3QP3/2B1n3/5N2/PPP1.text: But after we move our king Black has no further way to attack. Now Black will have to either lose the knight or get checkmated.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/3QP3/2B1n3/5N2/PPP2.text: Black takes with check and avoids losing material at the moment.

r1bqk2r/ppppbppp/2n5/2n1P3/2B5/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Black develops the bishop and gets ready to castle.

We'll develop the b1-knight towards the center.

r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/2p5/2n1P3/8/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
Black has to recapture. Otherwise, they have lost a whole piece.

White exchanges the queens and keeps the black king in the center. When our opponent's pawn structure is bad, the endgame usually suits us.

r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/2pp1n2/4P3/8/5N2/PPP2PP.text: White gains the sacrificed material back and opens up the central files that should give them access to the Black king.

r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/2pp1n2/4p3/3P4/5N2/PPP2.text: Black has to recapture. Otherwise, they have lost a whole piece.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3pp3/2BPP3/5N2/PP.text:
Black counterstrikes in the center and opens up their light-squared bishop.

We'll capture on d5, eliminating the attack on our bishop.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/2nBP3/8/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
Black moves the knight away and intends to put it on e6 to block the diagonal for our bishop.

We'll trade our d5-bishop for the knight in order to completely destroy Black's queenside pawn structure.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3n2N1/2Bp4/8/PPP2PP.text: White immediately puts pressure on f7 and intends to harass it more by bringing the queen to f3.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3n4/2Bp4/5N2/PPP2PP.text: Black is greedy and grabs pawns instead of focusing on quickly developing their pieces and castling.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3np3/2BP4/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Black recaptures the pawn and centralizes the knight.

We'll castle into safety before going on the attack.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3pP3/2B1n3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black opens up the bishop and protects the knight.

We'll just take on d5, reviving the threat to the knight.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/3Bp3/3P4/5N2/PPP.text:
Black pulls the loose knight back.

We'll continue our idea by capturing on c6 and undermining the e-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/4p3/2BPP3/5N2/PP.text:
Black fortifies the center and opens up the bishop. 

A small downside of the move is that the dark-squared bishop is blocked.

We'll castle our king into safety.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/8/2BpP3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black releases the tension in order to free e5 for the c6-knight.

We'll regain the pawn and centralize our knight by capturing on d4.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np4/4P3/2B1n3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black opens up the light-squared bishop, threatening our e5-pawn.

We'll punish Black's slow development by winning an important pawn with the temporary piece sacrifice Bxf7+!

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np4/4p3/2BPn3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black is greedy and captures a "free" pawn at the cost of their development.

We'll fork the two knights, intending to undermine Black's center by trading on c6.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3PN3/2Bn4/8/PPP2PPP.text:
White exploits Black's last move and grabs an important central pawn. 

Now Black has to spend time on getting their knight into safety, which should give White time to castle and start attacking black's king.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3Pp3/2Bn4/5N2/PPP2P.text: Black captures on d4 and moves the knight from c6, where it was under attack.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text:
Black responds with the Two Knights Defense.

Now we'll enter our gambit line by playing d4, gaining space in the center and forcing Black to react, plus opening up our dark-squared bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/2n1P3/2B5/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black pulls the knight back and intends to put it on e6 to block the white bishop.

We'll simply castle.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2BPn3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black takes the free pawn and hopes to get to play d5 on the next move in order to close the diagonal for our bishop and protect their king in the center.

We'll take on e5, opening up the d-file for the queen. The d5-square is very attractive, since the queen can threaten both f7 and e4 at the same time from there.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/2BnP3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black captures the d4-pawn and tries to keep the central files closed, but unfortunately for them, the e5-pawn is now unprotected.

With the neat Bxf7+, we'll immediately punish Black for leaving the defense of e5 by winning an important pawn and misplacing the black king.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black responds by developing their Knight and protecting the pawn.

With Bc4, we reach one of the most famous openings in chess - the Italian Game.

r2q1b1r/ppp2kpp/2npb3/3QP3/4n3/5N2/PPP2P.text: Black blocks the check and develops the bishop.

r2q1b1r/ppp2kpp/2npb3/4P3/4Q3/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
White regains the sacrificed piece with interest. If Black doesn't stop it, we are threatening Ng5+.

In the next few moves, White should castle and finish their queenside development. 

After that, it will be time to start harassing the exposed black king.

r2q1b1r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4N3/3nP1b1/8/PPPN1PP.text:
White unpins the knight with a check and will capture the bishop on the next move. 

With two extra pawns and Black's king not being able to castle, White should win the game without much effort.

r2q1b1r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/3nP1b1/5N2/PPPN1.text: Black's best option is to just go along with White's temporary sacrifice.

r2qk2r/p1p2ppp/2p5/2b1Pb2/4n3/5N2/PPP1QP.text: Black develops the final minor piece and gets ready to castle.
We castle the king into safety and will probably continue by developing the queenside and then bringing the rooks to the d- and e-files.

r2qkb1r/p1p2ppp/2p5/4Pb2/4n3/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
Black has to recapture. Otherwise, they have lost a whole piece.

We'll move the queen off the d-file in order to avoid trading queens.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P1b1/5N2/PP.text:
Black recaptures the pawn and offers a trade of queens in order to release the pressure.

We'll decline the queen trade and develop the knight, protecting e4 and f3.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3BPb2/4n3/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
Black develops the bishop and protects the knight on e4.

Let's capture on c6 and disrupt Black's pawns.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/4p3/2BPP1b1/5N2/P.text:
Black develops the bishop and pins the knight. The d4-pawn is now hanging.

We'll solve that problem by capturing on e5.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4n3/2B1P1b1/5N2/PP.text:
Black recaptures and threatens both our bishop and our knight on f3.

We'll retreat the bishop and add protection to the knight on f3. This secures our kingside pawn structure.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/8/4P1b1/5n2/PPP1BP.text:
Trading in order not to lose material is a better option for Black. 

We'll recapture with the bishop, maintaining the integrity of our pawn structure.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/8/4P3/5Q2/PPP2PPP/.text:
White recaptures the piece and develops the queen. 

In the next few moves, White will most likely develop the queenside and bring the rooks out.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/8/4P3/5b2/PPP2PPP/.text: Black does not want to retreat the bishop and waste more time, so they decide to trade it too.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p4/4N3/4n3/8/PPP1QPPP/R.text:
White recaptures with the queen and still wins a piece. 

If Black moves their knight, White will be able to make a nasty discovered check, and if Black takes on e5, then the knight on e4 falls.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p4/4N3/4n3/8/PPP1bPPP/R.text: If Black does not make this intermediate move, they lose a piece immediately.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p4/4n3/4n1b1/5N2/PPP1BP.text:
Black captures a pawn at the cost of their development.

We'll force trades in the center, leading to a sequence which wins material.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/4p3/2BnP1b1/5N2/PPPN.text:
Black takes advantage of the pin in order to centralize their knight.

But this is a mistake. We can win two pawns with a little combination. We sacrifice the bishop on f7, setting up a knight fork!

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
The most popular reply for Black.

With our response of Nf3, we are developing a piece, controlling the center, attacking the e5 pawn and are one move closer to castling.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
This study will continue looking at the Two Knights Double Gambit, but with deviations on the fourth move. 

The fourth move, just to give some context, is 4. d4, when we create our first pawn break. 

Let's see some side lines Black could go for after this!

We'll begin with 1.e4, "Best by test" - Bobby Fischer.
